summary: The Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness, where the devil tests what ‘Son of God’ will mean. Jesus answers three proposals with Deuteronomy, refusing provision, spectacle, and rule on the tester's terms. After John's arrest he settles in Capernaum, announces the kingdom in the same words John used, calls two pairs of fishermen, and begins teaching, proclaiming, and healing throughout Galilee.
whyItMatters: The beloved Son succeeds where Israel failed in the wilderness and refuses power severed from trust and worship. The chapter then gives Matthew a major transition — ‘from that time Jesus began’ — and compresses the ministry into a threefold pattern: teaching, proclaiming, and healing.

context.author: Anonymous Greek narrator arranging scriptural testing and ministry scenes
context.audience: Readers expected to recognize Deuteronomy and Isaiah inside the story
context.date: Late-first-century composition narrating the beginning of Jesus's Galilean ministry
context.setting: Wilderness, then Galilee around Capernaum under Herod Antipas
context.literaryForm: Scriptural contest followed by a programmatic ministry summary and call narratives

outline.heading: Bread and the meaning of sonship
Temple spectacle and world rule refused
Light in Galilee and kingdom proclamation

keyVerses.text: But he answered, “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth.’”
keyVerses.why: Jesus answers hunger by trusting the Scripture that interpreted Israel's wilderness dependence.

keyVerses.text: From that time, Jesus began to preach, and to say, “Repent! For the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand.”
keyVerses.why: A structural hinge begins the public ministry with the same kingdom summons John announced.

keyVerses.text: He said to them, “Come after me, and I will make you fishers for men.”
keyVerses.why: Discipleship starts as attachment to Jesus before it becomes a task performed for him.

questions.question: Is the devil ‘tempting’ Jesus to evil or ‘testing’ him?
questions.answer: Greek peirazō can mean test or tempt; context supplies the moral direction. The Spirit leads Jesus to be tested, while the devil tries to bend sonship toward distrust and false worship. The same event reveals faithfulness and carries temptation without suggesting the Spirit desires evil.

questions.question: Why does every answer come from Deuteronomy?
questions.answer: All three quotations come from Deuteronomy's reflection on Israel in the wilderness. Jesus has just been called God's Son and has passed through water; now, during forty days, he lives Israel's son-story faithfully. Matthew's point is not proof-text skill alone but a life governed by the story the quotations carry.

questions.question: Does ‘if you are the Son of God’ mean the tester doubts the title?
questions.answer: The Greek condition can work as ‘if, as claimed,’ not necessarily uncertainty. The pressure is about how sonship will be exercised: use power for self, force God to prove protection, or seize rule through compromise. Jesus refuses to let a true identity be defined by the wrong script.

questions.question: Why does the devil quote Scripture too?
questions.answer: At the temple the devil cites Psalm 91 accurately but tears protection away from trust and turns it into a demand for spectacle. Jesus answers with Scripture that forbids testing God. Matthew therefore rejects the idea that possessing a verse automatically guarantees faithful interpretation; context, purpose, and obedience matter.

questions.question: What does ‘from that time Jesus began’ signal?
questions.answer: Matthew uses the formula at major turns. Here it opens the Galilean proclamation; at 16:21 it opens the road toward suffering after Peter's confession. The repeated wording divides the Gospel's public movement into kingdom ministry and the explicit journey to the cross.

questions.question: What is a ‘gospel of the kingdom’?
questions.answer: Euangelion means good news or royal announcement, not yet a bound book called a Gospel. Jesus proclaims that God's reign has drawn near and demonstrates its character through teaching and healing. Matthew's summary makes word and deed interpret one another.

questions.question: Did the fishermen really follow a stranger without context?
questions.answer: Matthew narrates the calls with deliberate compression: Jesus commands and they respond ‘immediately.’ Other Gospel traditions describe earlier contact, but Matthew emphasizes authority and cost rather than the entire acquaintance. Nets, boat, father, and family livelihood make the response concrete, not romanticized poverty.

glossary.def: Greek and Semitic designations for the slanderer or adversary who tests Jesus's allegiance.
Isaiah's description of a northern border region shaped by conquest and mixed populations; Matthew frames Jesus's Galilean work as light.
Good news or royal announcement before it became the name for a written Jesus narrative.
